dataset.name: Dataset for Cruz-O'Bryne et al (2026): "Divergent biogeochemical responses in upland coastal forest soils to repeated flooding and shifts in water chemistry"
description: Hydrologic disturbances from accelerated sea-level rise and the increasing frequency and intensity of storms and tidal flooding are altering biogeochemical processes in upland coastal forests, transforming these ecosystems into wetlands. However, the initial effects of flooding on belowground biogeochemistry and the mechanisms driving greenhouse gas dynamics and soil organic matter stability during the early stages of this transition remain poorly understood. This dataset presents the results of a mesocosm experiment conducted in a controlled, highly instrumented laboratory environment, in which freshwater and brackish water pulses were applied to intact soil monoliths from a temperate upland coastal forest to examine how floodwater chemistry influences soil biogeochemistry and organo-mineral interactions.
All data files are plain-text CSV (comma-separated value), and no special software is required to read them. Details about the content of each file are available in the document “Dataset_readme”.
The dataset consists of the following data:
• rcruzobyrne_GHG: Headspace greenhouse gas (GHG) concentration and fluxes
• rcruzobyrne_CDOM: Porewater colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM)

Details of the experimental setup, data collection, and data analysis are provided in the manuscript by Cruz-O’Byrne et al (2026) Divergent biogeochemical responses in upland coastal forest soils to repeated flooding and shifts in water chemistry. Under review in Biogeochemistry.

measurementTechnique:
Samples and experimental phases: Duplicate intact soil monoliths (22 cm depth x 22 cm diameter) were collected from each TEMPEST treatment plot (C, FW, BW) using PVC collars fixed on high-density polyethylene boards. Municipal water (fresh water) and estuarine water (brackish water) were used to simulate flooding events under laboratory conditions.
The mesocosm experiment lasted 50 days (N) and was divided into eight phases:
• Phase I: Pre-experiment – Baseline monitoring (N < 5.85)
• Phase II: DI water pulse for all mesocosms (5.85 ≤ N ≤ 6.27)
• Phase III: Soil recovery 1 – Soil drainage (6.27 < N < 13.2)
• Phase IV: FW/BW pulse, except C mesocosms (13.2 ≤ N ≤ 16.27)
• Phase V: Soil recovery 2 – Soil drainage (16.27 < N < 22.92)
• Phase VI: DI water pulse for all mesocosms (22.92 ≤ N ≤ 23.34)
• Phase VII: Soil recovery 3 – Soil drainage until CO₂ convergence (23.34 < N < 29.94)
• Phase VIII: Post-experiment – Soil drying (N ≥ 29.94)

Experimental setup and data collection: Soil monoliths (mesocosms) were maintained in a controlled laboratory environment at 22.0 ± 1.7 °C. Peristaltic pumps supplied water and controlled outflow to simulate soil hydrology connectivity.
• Soil moisture at 5 cm depth was recorded every 30 min using ECH2O EC-5 sensors (METER Group, Pullman, WA, USA). The dataset is reported as raw.
• Greenhouse gas fluxes (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) were measured every 30 min with automated chambers (LI-8200-104, LI-COR, Lincoln, NE, USA) connected to an analyzer (G2508, Picarro, Santa Clara, CA). Soil greenhouse gas fluxes were calculated using SoilFluxPro™ (v.5.3, LI-COR, Lincoln, NE, USA). Linear and exponential models were fitted, and fluxes were selected based on the highest R². Fluxes were retained only when the corresponding CO₂ fit had R² > 0.9 during baseline periods or > 0.8 during water pulses; otherwise, fluxes for all gases were set to NaN. Missing values were subsequently gap-filled using an iterative rolling mean (window size = 3) implemented with the Pandas library (v. 2.2.2) in Python. The dataset is reported as raw concentration and processed fluxes.
• Discrete chamber air samples were collected for δ¹³C-CH₄ analysis using a Cavity Ring-Down Spectrometer (G2201-i, Picarro, Santa Clara, CA), connected to a Small Sample Introduction Module (SSIM2/A0314, Picarro, Santa Clara, CA). Standards and zero-air blanks were analyzed at the beginning and end of each analytical day to verify accuracy and drift. The dataset is reported as raw.
• Porewater (15 mL) was sampled at 5 cm depth with Rhizon samplers and analyzed for DOC, DIC, HS⁻, SO₄²⁻, Fe²⁺, Mn²⁺, NH₃, NH₄⁺, and NO₃⁻ + NO₂⁻, Eh, pH. The dataset is reported as the mean ± standard deviation for duplicates by sampling point for each treatment.
• Additional porewater (10 mL) was sampled during flooding phases (II, IV, and VI) and used for spectroscopy analysis of CDOM using an Aqualog spectrofluorometer (Horiba Scientific, New Jersey, USA) with a 10-mm quartz cuvette (Starna Cells, Atascadero, CA). Daily, fresh MilliQ water was used to collect blank spectra, which were later subtracted from the sample spectra to ensure data accuracy. The dataset is reported as the mean ± standard deviation for duplicates by experimental phase for each treatment.
• Soil samples were collected before and after the mesocosm experiment to analyze functional groups using an FTIR spectrometer (Nicolet 6700, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) equipped with a DTGS-KBr detector using the KBr pellet method. The dataset is reported as raw absorbance.

More details on experimental setup, data collection, methods, and data analysis are provided in the manuscript by Cruz-O’Byrne et al (2026) Divergent biogeochemical responses in upland coastal forest soils to repeated flooding and shifts in water chemistry. Under review in Biogeochemistry.
